claim: Deletion of the chromatin regulator Kdm6a (Utx) in the paternal germ line results in elevated tumor incidence in genetically wild type mice.
source: We report that deletion of the chromatin regulator Kdm6a (Utx) in the paternal germ line results in elevated tumor incidence in genetically wild type mice.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by survival and tumor incidence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of Kdm6a deletion on tumor incidence increases following passage through two successive generations of Kdm6a male germline deletion.
source: This effect increases following passage through two successive generations of Kdm6a male germline deletion, but is lost following passage through a wild type germ line.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by F2 generation data showing enhanced tumor phenotypes.

claim: The tumor susceptibility effect is lost following passage through a wild type germ line.
source: This effect increases following passage through two successive generations of Kdm6a male germline deletion, but is lost following passage through a wild type germ line.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by control F2 data showing no increased tumor burden.

claim: The H3K27me3 mark is redistributed in sperm of Kdm6a mutants.
source: The H3K27me3 mark is redistributed in sperm of Kdm6a mutants, and we define approximately 200 H3K27me3-marked regions that exhibit increased DNA methylation, both in sperm of Kdm6a mutants and in somatic tissue of progeny.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by ChIP-seq data showing altered H3K27me3 distribution in Kdm6a cKO sperm.

claim: Approximately 200 H3K27me3-marked regions exhibit increased DNA methylation in both sperm of Kdm6a mutants and in somatic tissue of progeny.
source: The H3K27me3 mark is redistributed in sperm of Kdm6a mutants, and we define approximately 200 H3K27me3-marked regions that exhibit increased DNA methylation, both in sperm of Kdm6a mutants and in somatic tissue of progeny.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by RRBS data showing persistent hypermethylated DMRs (207 regions).

claim: Hypermethylated regions in enhancers may alter regulation of genes involved in cancer initiation or progression.
source: Hypermethylated regions in enhancers may alter regulation of genes involved in cancer initiation or progression.
evidence: The abstract states this as a speculative conclusion based on the proximity of persistent DMRs to enhancers and enrichment for tumorigenesis-related phenotypes.

claim: Epigenetic changes in male gametes may impact cancer susceptibility in adult offspring.
source: Epigenetic changes in male gametes may therefore impact cancer susceptibility in adult offspring.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement, which is supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: Intergenerational inheritance of epigenetic state may significantly impact disease susceptibility in animals, including humans.
source: Intergenerational inheritance of epigenetic state may significantly impact disease susceptibility in animals, including humans.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general principle supported by accumulating evidence from the literature.

claim: Male and female gametes transmit epigenetic regulatory information in the form of covalent DNA modification, histone modification, and small RNAs to the zygote at fertilization.
source: In addition to genetic information, male and female gametes transmit epigenetic regulatory information, in the form of covalent DNA modification, histone modification, and small RNAs, to the zygote at fertilization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Epigenetic information inherited from both maternal and paternal gametes can modulate gene expression and phenotype in progeny throughout the metazoan lineage.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that the epigenetic information inherited from both maternal and paternal gametes can modulate gene expression and phenotype in progeny throughout the metazoan lineage (Arico et al., 2011; Carone et al., 2010; Ciabrelli et al., 2017; Greer et al., 2011; Morgan et al., 1999; Siklenka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcriptional effects from epigenetic inheritance can manifest phenotypically as defects in early development.
source: In mammals, these transcriptional effects can manifest phenotypically as defects in early development (Chong et al., 2007; Siklenka et al., 2015) or as altered metabolic or behavioral states during adulthood (Carone et al., 2010; Dias and Ressler, 2014; Ng et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcriptional effects from epigenetic inheritance can manifest as altered metabolic or behavioral states during adulthood.
source: In mammals, these transcriptional effects can manifest phenotypically as defects in early development (Chong et al., 2007; Siklenka et al., 2015) or as altered metabolic or behavioral states during adulthood (Carone et al., 2010; Dias and Ressler, 2014; Ng et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mature mammalian sperm exhibit relatively high levels of DNA methylation.
source: Mature mammalian sperm exhibit relatively high levels of DNA methylation (Monk et al., 1987), contain populations of small RNAs (Sharma et al., 2016; Siklenka et al., 2015), and retain 5–10% of their histones (Hammoud et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2017), which bear extensive post-translational modifications (Erkek et al., 2013; Hammoud et al., 2009; Luense et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Monk et al., 1987.

claim: Mature mammalian sperm contain populations of small RNAs.
source: Mature mammalian sperm exhibit relatively high levels of DNA methylation (Monk et al., 1987), contain populations of small RNAs (Sharma et al., 2016; Siklenka et al., 2015), and retain 5–10% of their histones (Hammoud et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2017), which bear extensive post-translational modifications (Erkek et al., 2013; Hammoud et al., 2009; Luense et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2016 and Siklenka et al., 2015.

claim: Mature mammalian sperm retain 5–10% of their histones.
source: Mature mammalian sperm exhibit relatively high levels of DNA methylation (Monk et al., 1987), contain populations of small RNAs (Sharma et al., 2016; Siklenka et al., 2015), and retain 5–10% of their histones (Hammoud et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2017), which bear extensive post-translational modifications (Erkek et al., 2013; Hammoud et al., 2009; Luense et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hammoud et al., 2009 and Jung et al., 2017.

claim: Retained histones in sperm bear extensive post-translational modifications.
source: Mature mammalian sperm exhibit relatively high levels of DNA methylation (Monk et al., 1987), contain populations of small RNAs (Sharma et al., 2016; Siklenka et al., 2015), and retain 5–10% of their histones (Hammoud et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2017), which bear extensive post-translational modifications (Erkek et al., 2013; Hammoud et al., 2009; Luense et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Erkek et al., 2013, Hammoud et al., 2009, and Luense et al., 2016.

claim: Specific histone modifications at some loci in the male germ line have been conserved during mammalian evolution.
source: Specific histone modifications at some loci in the male germ line have been conserved during mammalian evolution, implying a biologically important function (Lesch et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lesch et al., 2016.

claim: Conservation of specific histone modifications in the male germ line implies a biologically important function.
source: Specific histone modifications at some loci in the male germ line have been conserved during mammalian evolution, implying a biologically important function (Lesch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of evolutionary conservation.

claim: Mature mouse sperm retain elements of large-scale three-dimensional genomic domains found in somatic cells.
source: Recent evidence suggests that mature mouse sperm also retain elements of large-scale three-dimensional genomic domains found in somatic cells (Jung et al., 2017; Ke et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jung et al., 2017 and Ke et al., 2017.

claim: Altered epigenetic states play a significant role in cancer pathogenesis.
source: Altered epigenetic states play a significant role in cancer pathogenesis, making cancer a strong candidate for sensitivity to intergenerational epigenetic effects.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many cancers are highly heritable.
source: Many cancers are highly heritable, meaning that the presence of a given tumor or set of tumors in one individual increases the risk of developing the same tumors among close relatives (Goldgar et al., 1994; Lichtenstein et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Goldgar et al., 1994 and Lichtenstein et al., 2000.

claim: A large fraction of cancer heritability remains unexplained by specific genetic mutations or variants.
source: However, despite extensive genetic studies of many human cancers, a large fraction of this heritability remains unexplained by specific genetic mutations or variants (Lichtenstein et al., 2000; Mucci et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lichtenstein et al., 2000 and Mucci et al., 2016.

claim: Many tumors are characterized by significantly perturbed gene regulatory states and exhibit abnormal genome-wide histone methylation and DNA methylation profiles.
source: Many tumors are characterized by significantly perturbed gene regulatory states and exhibit abnormal genome-wide histone methylation and DNA methylation profiles (Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012.

claim: When cancer susceptibility genes can be identified, many encode chromatin regulators.
source: Cancer genetics studies over the last decade have revealed that, when susceptibility genes can be identified, many encode chromatin regulators, implying that epigenetic changes contribute either to tumor initiation or tumor progression (Baylin and Jones, 2011; Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baylin and Jones, 2011 and Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012.

claim: Epigenetic changes contribute to tumor initiation or tumor progression.
source: Cancer genetics studies over the last decade have revealed that, when susceptibility genes can be identified, many encode chromatin regulators, implying that epigenetic changes contribute either to tumor initiation or tumor progression (Baylin and Jones, 2011; Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that many cancer susceptibility genes encode chromatin regulators.

claim: Kdm6a (Utx) has been identified as a candidate tumor suppressor in cancer genetics studies.
source: Kdm6a (Utx) has been identified as a candidate tumor suppressor in cancer genetics studies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations to cancer genetics studies.

claim: The KDM6A protein has histone demethylase activity toward lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27).
source: The KDM6A protein has histone demethylase activity toward lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27), as well as demethylase-independent functions in establishment of enhancer regions (Hong et al., 2007; Lan et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2007 and Lan et al., 2007.

claim: KDM6A has demethylase-independent functions in establishment of enhancer regions.
source: The KDM6A protein has histone demethylase activity toward lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27), as well as demethylase-independent functions in establishment of enhancer regions (Hong et al., 2007; Lan et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2007, Lan et al., 2007, and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: KDM6A mutations are found in multiple myeloma, renal cell carcinoma, bladder carcinoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL), prostate cancer, and medulloblastoma.
source: KDM6A mutations are found in a variety of human cancers, including multiple myeloma, renal cell carcinoma, bladder carcinoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL), prostate cancer, and medulloblastoma (Jones et al., 2012; Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2014; van Haaften et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2012, Ntziachristos et al., 2014, Van der Meulen et al., 2014, and van Haaften et al., 2009.

claim: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL.
source: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL (Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2015), AML (Gozdecka et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Wu et al., 2018), and also plays important developmental roles, especially in the heart (Lee et al., 2012; Welstead et al., 2012) and blood (Beyaz et al., 2017; Thieme et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ntziachristos et al., 2014 and Van der Meulen et al., 2015.

claim: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in AML.
source: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL (Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2015), AML (Gozdecka et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Wu et al., 2018), and also plays important developmental roles, especially in the heart (Lee et al., 2012; Welstead et al., 2012) and blood (Beyaz et al., 2017; Thieme et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gozdecka et al., 2018.

claim: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in lung cancer.
source: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL (Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2015), AML (Gozdecka et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Wu et al., 2018), and also plays important developmental roles, especially in the heart (Lee et al., 2012; Welstead et al., 2012) and blood (Beyaz et al., 2017; Thieme et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2018.

claim: KDM6A plays important developmental roles in the heart.
source: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL (Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2015), AML (Gozdecka et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Wu et al., 2018), and also plays important developmental roles, especially in the heart (Lee et al., 2012; Welstead et al., 2012) and blood (Beyaz et al., 2017; Thieme et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012 and Welstead et al., 2012.

claim: KDM6A plays important developmental roles in blood.
source: KDM6A has been mechanistically implicated as a tumor suppressor in ALL (Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Van der Meulen et al., 2015), AML (Gozdecka et al., 2018), and lung cancer (Wu et al., 2018), and also plays important developmental roles, especially in the heart (Lee et al., 2012; Welstead et al., 2012) and blood (Beyaz et al., 2017; Thieme et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beyaz et al., 2017 and Thieme et al., 2013.

claim: The epigenetic sequelae of KDM6A loss contribute to tumor initiation or progression.
source: Because KDM6A functions primarily as a chromatin regulator, these studies imply that the epigenetic sequelae of KDM6A loss contribute to tumor initiation or progression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that KDM6A functions as a chromatin regulator and is implicated in cancer.

claim: Mating Kdm6a cKO males to wild-type females produced genetically wild type male offspring and heterozygous female offspring.
source: Mating Kdm6a cKO males to wild-type females produced genetically wild type male offspring ('Kdm6a F1') and heterozygous female offspring (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, describing the breeding strategy.

claim: Kdm6a F1 males are genetically wild type but generated from a paternal germ line lacking KDM6A activity.
source: Critically, Kdm6a F1 males are genetically wild type, but generated from a paternal germ line lacking KDM6A activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a critical feature of the experimental design.

claim: Kdm6a cKO males were fertile.
source: Kdm6a cKO males were fertile, produced male and female offspring at Mendelian ratios, and exhibited normal spermatogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kdm6a cKO males produced male and female offspring at Mendelian ratios.
source: Kdm6a cKO males were fertile, produced male and female offspring at Mendelian ratios, and exhibited normal spermatogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kdm6a cKO males exhibited normal spermatogenesis.
source: Kdm6a cKO males were fertile, produced male and female offspring at Mendelian ratios, and exhibited normal spermatogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by histological images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The efficiency of Cre recombinase activity was greater than 97%.
source: We confirmed the high efficiency of Cre recombinase activity (>97%) by genotyping the heterozygous female offspring of these crosses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genotyping data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lifespans of Kdm6a F1 males were shorter than those of control F1s.
source: We found that lifespans of Kdm6a F1 males were shorter than those of control F1s (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival curves in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The survival difference between Kdm6a F1 and control F1 males was independent of whether the animal carried the Ddx4-Cre transgene.
source: This effect was independent of whether the animal carried the Ddx4-Cre transgene (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and of mode of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The survival difference between Kdm6a F1 and control F1 males was independent of mode of death.
source: This effect was independent of whether the animal carried the Ddx4-Cre transgene (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and of mode of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: There was no significant difference in weight between Kdm6a F1s and control F1s at the time of death.
source: There was no significant difference in weight and a mild reduction in body length for Kdm6a F1s compared to control F1s at the time of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: There was a mild reduction in body length for Kdm6a F1s compared to control F1s at the time of death.
source: There was no significant difference in weight and a mild reduction in body length for Kdm6a F1s compared to control F1s at the time of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Kdm6a F1s that died between 12 and 18 months of age did not exhibit evidence of a unifying disease process.
source: We found that Kdm6a F1s that died between 12 and 18 months of age did not exhibit evidence of a unifying disease process.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on evaluation of necropsy data.

claim: Kdm6a F1s that died between 18 and 24 months of age exhibited an increased tumor burden compared to age-matched control F1s.
source: In contrast, Kdm6a F1s that died between 18 and 24 months of age exhibited an increased tumor burden compared to age-matched control F1s (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The spectrum of tumors identified in Kdm6a F1s was similar to that observed in normally aging mice.
source: The spectrum of tumors identified was similar to that observed in normally aging mice (Haines et al., 2001), but appeared earlier and at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Haines et al., 2001 for comparison.

claim: Tumors in Kdm6a F1s appeared earlier and at higher frequencies than in normally aging mice.
source: The spectrum of tumors identified was similar to that observed in normally aging mice (Haines et al., 2001), but appeared earlier and at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on comparison with published data on normally aging mice.

claim: The most common cancer type in Kdm6a F1s was histiocytic sarcoma.
source: The most common cancer type was histiocytic sarcoma, a blood tumor of the monocyte/macrophage lineage (Figure 1D; 6/22 vs. 1/25 mice, p=0.040, Fisher's Exact test); this tumor was found in Kdm6a F1s at a mean age of 624 ± 61 days, and in a single control F1 at 722 days.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by histological images in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Histiocytic sarcoma occurred in 6 out of 22 Kdm6a F1 mice compared to 1 out of 25 control F1 mice (p=0.040).
source: The most common cancer type was histiocytic sarcoma, a blood tumor of the monocyte/macrophage lineage (Figure 1D; 6/22 vs. 1/25 mice, p=0.040, Fisher's Exact test); this tumor was found in Kdm6a F1s at a mean age of 624 ± 61 days, and in a single control F1 at 722 days.
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Histiocytic sarcoma was found in Kdm6a F1s at a mean age of 624 ± 61 days.
source: The most common cancer type was histiocytic sarcoma, a blood tumor of the monocyte/macrophage lineage (Figure 1D; 6/22 vs. 1/25 mice, p=0.040, Fisher's Exact test); this tumor was found in Kdm6a F1s at a mean age of 624 ± 61 days, and in a single control F1 at 722 days.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of necropsy data.

claim: Flow cytometry of bone marrow from Kdm6a F1 mice revealed expanded populations of monocyte-lineage cells.
source: Flow cytometry of bone marrow from these mice revealed expanded populations of monocyte-lineage cells, consistent with histiocytic sarcoma.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Kdm6a F1 mice not identified as having histiocytic sarcoma by histopathology had a moderate increase in monocyte-lineage cell populations.
source: In addition, Kdm6a F1 mice not identified as having histiocytic sarcoma by histopathology also had a moderate increase in monocyte-lineage cell populations, indicating subtle skewing of hematopoietic lineages even in the absence of full-blown disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: Kdm6a F2s exhibited reduced survival relative to the original control F1 cohort.
source: We found that, like Kdm6a F1s, Kdm6a F2s exhibited reduced survival relative to the original control F1 cohort, whereas survival of control F2 males was more variable (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival curves in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Survival of control F2 males was more variable than Kdm6a F2s.
source: We found that, like Kdm6a F1s, Kdm6a F2s exhibited reduced survival relative to the original control F1 cohort, whereas survival of control F2 males was more variable (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival curves in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kdm6a F2s had an increased tumor burden relative to the F1 control cohort.
source: Also like Kdm6a F1s, Kdm6a F2s had an increased tumor burden relative to the F1 control cohort (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no evidence for increased tumor burden in control F2 males.
source: We did not find evidence for increased tumor burden in control F2 males.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of necropsy data.

claim: Repeated loss of Kdm6a in the male germ line is required to maintain the intergenerational tumor susceptibility phenotype.
source: We conclude that repeated loss of Kdm6a in the male germ line is required to maintain the intergenerational tumor susceptibility phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that control F2s (with one generation of wild-type Kdm6a) do not show increased tumor burden.

claim: The tumor phenotype was more pronounced in Kdm6a F2s compared to Kdm6a F1s.
source: Notably, the tumor phenotype was more pronounced in Kdm6a F2s compared to Kdm6a F1s: Kdm6a F2s developed more tumors per mouse (overall tumor rate: 0.24 control, 0.95 Kdm6a F1, 1.30 Kdm6a F2; Figure 2—source data 2), and when present, tumors were more aggressive.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by tumor count data.

claim: Kdm6a F2s developed more tumors per mouse than Kdm6a F1s (overall tumor rate: 0.24 control, 0.95 Kdm6a F1, 1.30 Kdm6a F2).
source: Notably, the tumor phenotype was more pronounced in Kdm6a F2s compared to Kdm6a F1s: Kdm6a F2s developed more tumors per mouse (overall tumor rate: 0.24 control, 0.95 Kdm6a F1, 1.30 Kdm6a F2; Figure 2—source data 2), and when present, tumors were more aggressive.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific tumor rates provided.

claim: Thirty-eight percent (15/40) of Kdm6a F2 mice had more than one independent tumor at death.
source: Thirty-eight percent (15/40) of Kdm6a F2 mice had more than one independent tumor at death, compared to 23% (5/22) of Kdm6a F1 mice and 4% (1/25) of control F1 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Twenty-three percent (5/22) of Kdm6a F1 mice had more than one independent tumor at death.
source: Thirty-eight percent (15/40) of Kdm6a F2 mice had more than one independent tumor at death, compared to 23% (5/22) of Kdm6a F1 mice and 4% (1/25) of control F1 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Four percent (1/25) of control F1 mice had more than one independent tumor at death.
source: Thirty-eight percent (15/40) of Kdm6a F2 mice had more than one independent tumor at death, compared to 23% (5/22) of Kdm6a F1 mice and 4% (1/25) of control F1 mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: A higher fraction of Kdm6a F2 tumors were malignant compared to Kdm6a F1 tumors.
source: In addition, a higher fraction of Kdm6a F2 tumors were malignant (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: Exposure of male germ cells to loss of Kdm6a across multiple generations confers a cumulative risk of tumor development on offspring.
source: We conclude that exposure of male germ cells to loss of Kdm6a across multiple generations confers a cumulative risk of tumor development on offspring.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that F2 mice show more severe tumor phenotypes than F1 mice.

claim: Molecular changes mediating the tumor susceptibility effect accumulate across generations.
source: These findings imply that the molecular changes mediating this effect accumulate across generations, but can be reset when germline Kdm6a expression is restored.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that F2 mice show enhanced phenotypes and control F2 mice do not.

claim: Molecular changes mediating the tumor susceptibility effect can be reset when germline Kdm6a expression is restored.
source: These findings imply that the molecular changes mediating this effect accumulate across generations, but can be reset when germline Kdm6a expression is restored.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that control F2 mice (with restored Kdm6a) do not show increased tumor burden.

claim: There was an increase in H3K27me3 signal in Kdm6a cKO sperm relative to control sperm after normalizing for library size.
source: Genome-wide, we observed an increase in H3K27me3 signal in Kdm6a cKO sperm relative to control sperm after normalizing for library size, as expected for loss of an H3K27me3 demethylase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: A global gain in H3K27me3 in Kdm6a cKO sperm was confirmed by Western blot.
source: We confirmed a global gain in H3K27me3 by Western blot (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: The increase in H3K27me3 was not uniform throughout the genome in Kdm6a cKO sperm.
source: However, this effect was not uniform throughout the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Tiles with the highest overall H3K27me3 signal exhibited a paradoxical loss of H3K27me3 in Kdm6a cKOs.
source: While H3K27me3 signal increased in the majority of tiles in Kdm6a cKO sperm, those tiles with the highest overall H3K27me3 signal exhibited a paradoxical loss of H3K27me3 in Kdm6a cKOs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of KDM6A results in an apparent flattening of the H3K27me3 profile.
source: The result is an apparent flattening of the H3K27me3 profile: a decrease in H3K27me3 at regions with high signal, accompanied by an increase in H3K27me3 in adjacent regions (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplements 4–5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplements 4-5.

claim: Loss of KDM6A increases H3K27me3 overall and alters the normal pattern of distribution of H3K27me3 during spermatogenesis.
source: Allowing for each of these explanations, we conclude that loss of KDM6A increases H3K27me3 overall and alters the normal pattern of distribution of H3K27me3 during spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Regions where H3K27me3 was altered in Kdm6a cKO sperm were associated with increased DNA methylation.
source: However, regions where H3K27me3 was altered, defined as those tiles with log2 fold change >0.5 or<−0.5 and false discovery rate <0.1 in both ChIP-seq replicates and which were not called as different in comparisons between the two control or two cKO datasets, were associated with increased DNA methylation (Figure 3F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3F, 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplements 6-7.

claim: Both increased and decreased H3K27me3 were associated with a gain in DNA methylation.
source: Both increased and decreased H3K27me3 were associated with a gain in DNA methylation, possibly due to secondary alterations in histone methylation after establishment of an initial change in DNA methylation.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of RRBS data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Regions with altered H3K27me3 were enriched near gene bodies.
source: These regions were enriched near gene bodies (p=9.898×10−6 for H3K27me3 gain and p=5.892×10−4 for H3K27me3 loss, Fisher's exact test), and regions of H3K27me3 loss were also weakly enriched at transcription start sites (p=0.01368, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Regions of H3K27me3 loss were weakly enriched at transcription start sites.
source: These regions were enriched near gene bodies (p=9.898×10−6 for H3K27me3 gain and p=5.892×10−4 for H3K27me3 loss, Fisher's exact test), and regions of H3K27me3 loss were also weakly enriched at transcription start sites (p=0.01368, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Genes exhibiting loss of H3K27me3 and gain of DNA methylation were enriched for functions such as 'negative regulation of myeloid dendritic cell activation' and 'positive regulation of immune effector process'.
source: Genes exhibiting loss of H3K27me3 and gain of DNA methylation were enriched for functions such as 'negative regulation of myeloid dendritic cell activation' and 'positive regulation of immune effector process' (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by gene ontology analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: Deletion of Kdm6a early in spermatogenesis induces redistribution of H3K27me3.
source: Together, our results indicate that deletion of Kdm6a early in spermatogenesis induces redistribution of H3K27me3, and that regions strongly affected by H3K27me3 redistribution gain DNA methylation in mature sperm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq and RRBS data.

claim: Regions strongly affected by H3K27me3 redistribution gain DNA methylation in mature sperm.
source: Together, our results indicate that deletion of Kdm6a early in spermatogenesis induces redistribution of H3K27me3, and that regions strongly affected by H3K27me3 redistribution gain DNA methylation in mature sperm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq and RRBS data.

claim: DMRs in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were more likely to be hypermethylated than hypomethylated relative to their respective controls.
source: DMRs in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were more likely to be hypermethylated than hypomethylated relative to their respective controls (4725 hypermethylated vs. 323 hypomethylated DMRs in sperm and 3156 hypermethylated vs. 1122 hypomethylated DMRs in bone marrow).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific counts of DMRs.

claim: Two hundred and ninety-nine regions were differentially methylated in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow.
source: Two hundred and ninety-nine regions were differentially methylated in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, significantly more than expected by chance (57 regions expected, p=4.22e-121, hypergeometric test) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The overlap of 299 DMRs between sperm and bone marrow was significantly more than expected by chance (p=4.22e-121).
source: Two hundred and ninety-nine regions were differentially methylated in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, significantly more than expected by chance (57 regions expected, p=4.22e-121, hypergeometric test) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the magnitude of DNA methylation change in sperm and in F1 bone marrow for the 299 shared DMRs (R = 0.17, p=0.0026).
source: Considering all 299 shared DMRs, there was a positive correlation between the magnitude of DNA methylation change in sperm and in F1 bone marrow (R = 0.17, p=0.0026) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Two hundred and twenty-six individual DMRs (76%) were positively correlated between sperm and F1 bone marrow.
source: Two hundred and twenty-six individual DMRs (76%) were positively correlated between sperm and F1 bone marrow, including 207 (69%) hypermethylated and 19 (6%) hypomethylated regions (Figure 4—source data 3, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of RRBS data.

claim: Hypermethylation was validated at 12 of 13 tested DMRs in at least one tissue using pyrosequencing.
source: We validated our RRBS findings using pyrosequencing in Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, and confirmed hypermethylation at 12 of 13 tested DMRs in at least one tissue and at seven of 13 DMRs in both tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pyrosequencing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hypermethylation was validated at 7 of 13 tested DMRs in both sperm and bone marrow using pyrosequencing.
source: We validated our RRBS findings using pyrosequencing in Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, and confirmed hypermethylation at 12 of 13 tested DMRs in at least one tissue and at seven of 13 DMRs in both tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pyrosequencing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Persistent DMRs were distributed throughout the genome.
source: We found that persistent DMRs were distributed throughout the genome (Figure 4D) and frequently overlapped the regions of greatest H3K27me3 change in Kdm6a cKO sperm (Figures 3F and 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Persistent DMRs frequently overlapped the regions of greatest H3K27me3 change in Kdm6a cKO sperm.
source: We found that persistent DMRs were distributed throughout the genome (Figure 4D) and frequently overlapped the regions of greatest H3K27me3 change in Kdm6a cKO sperm (Figures 3F and 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 3F and 4E.

claim: There was no association between persistent DMRs and CpG islands.
source: In contrast, there was no association between persistent DMRs and various other features, including CpG islands, imprinted regions, and transcription start sites (TSS) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no association between persistent DMRs and imprinted regions.
source: In contrast, there was no association between persistent DMRs and various other features, including CpG islands, imprinted regions, and transcription start sites (TSS) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no association between persistent DMRs and transcription start sites.
source: In contrast, there was no association between persistent DMRs and various other features, including CpG islands, imprinted regions, and transcription start sites (TSS) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Persistent DMRs were not more likely to overlap repetitive elements compared to the complete set of genomic regions covered by RRBS data.
source: Although repetitive elements such as retrotransposons can be resistant to DNA methylation reprogramming in the germ line (Guibert et al., 2012), persistent DMRs were not more likely to overlap repetitive elements compared to the complete set of genomic regions covered by our RRBS data (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: The location of persistent DMRs is strongly associated with regions of altered H3K27me3 in sperm.
source: We conclude that the location of persistent DMRs is strongly associated with regions of altered H3K27me3 in sperm, implying that loss of Kdm6a in the male germ line sensitizes these regions to DNA hypermethylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of DMR locations relative to H3K27me3 changes.

claim: Loss of Kdm6a in the male germ line sensitizes regions with altered H3K27me3 to DNA hypermethylation.
source: We conclude that the location of persistent DMRs is strongly associated with regions of altered H3K27me3 in sperm, implying that loss of Kdm6a in the male germ line sensitizes these regions to DNA hypermethylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association between persistent DMRs and regions of altered H3K27me3.

claim: Some regions that are sensitized to DNA hypermethylation may retain their methylation state during somatic development in the next generation.
source: Some of these sensitive regions may retain their methylation state during somatic development in the next generation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of persistent DMRs in F1 bone marrow.

claim: Persistent DMRs were close to or overlapping both poised and active enhancer regions in bone marrow, bone marrow macrophages, and round spermatids.
source: We found that persistent DMRs were close to or overlapping both poised (marked by H3K4me1) and active (marked by both H3K4me1 and H3K27ac) enhancer regions in all three of these tissues or cell types (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The top ten most strongly enriched mouse phenotypes associated with persistent DMRs were all related to tumorigenesis.
source: The top ten most strongly enriched mouse phenotypes were all related to tumorigenesis, including 'increased classified tumor incidence', 'altered tumor susceptibility', and 'malignant tumors' (Figure 4I–J, Figure 4—figure supplements 4–5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4I-J and Figure 4—figure supplements 4-5.

claim: Kdm6a-dependent hypermethylated persistent DMRs affect enhancer regions relevant to tumorigenesis in mice.
source: We conclude that Kdm6a-dependent hypermethylated persistent DMRs affect enhancer regions relevant to tumorigenesis in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proximity of persistent DMRs to enhancers and enrichment for tumorigenesis-related phenotypes.

claim: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 140 (67%) were also found in liver tumors.
source: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 140 (67%, OR 87.32, p<2.2e-16) were also found in liver tumors, and 68 (35%, OR 408.65, p<2.2e-16) were also found in spleen, and the magnitudes of DNA methylation changes were positively correlated: R = 0.232 (liver) and R = 0.786 (spleen).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 68 (35%) were also found in spleen.
source: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 140 (67%, OR 87.32, p<2.2e-16) were also found in liver tumors, and 68 (35%, OR 408.65, p<2.2e-16) were also found in spleen, and the magnitudes of DNA methylation changes were positively correlated: R = 0.232 (liver) and R = 0.786 (spleen).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: The magnitudes of DNA methylation changes at persistent DMRs were positively correlated between bone marrow and liver tumors (R = 0.232).
source: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 140 (67%, OR 87.32, p<2.2e-16) were also found in liver tumors, and 68 (35%, OR 408.65, p<2.2e-16) were also found in spleen, and the magnitudes of DNA methylation changes were positively correlated: R = 0.232 (liver) and R = 0.786 (spleen).
evidence: This is stated in the text with correlation coefficient provided.

claim: The magnitudes of DNA methylation changes at persistent DMRs were positively correlated between bone marrow and spleen (R = 0.786).
source: Of the 207 persistent DMRs detected in bone marrow, 140 (67%, OR 87.32, p<2.2e-16) were also found in liver tumors, and 68 (35%, OR 408.65, p<2.2e-16) were also found in spleen, and the magnitudes of DNA methylation changes were positively correlated: R = 0.232 (liver) and R = 0.786 (spleen).
evidence: This is stated in the text with correlation coefficient provided.

claim: The similarity of methylation changes across different tissues supports the model that these changes were present in the early embryo and persisted during lineage commitment and organ differentiation.
source: The similarity of methylation changes across different tissues supports the model that these changes were present in the early embryo and persisted during lineage commitment and organ differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar methylation changes across multiple tissues.

claim: Persistent DMRs contain enriched binding sites for the ETS transcription factors ELK1, ELK4, and GABPA.
source: We detected enrichment of binding sites corresponding to the ETS transcription factors ELK1, ELK4, and GABPA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by motif enrichment analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: DNA methylation reduces the affinity of ELK1, ELK4, and GABPA for their binding sites.
source: DNA methylation reduces the affinity of all three of these factors for their binding sites (Yin et al., 2017), implying that persistent hypermethylation at these sites can impact expression of downstream genes in F1 somatic tissue.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2017.

claim: Persistent hypermethylation at ELK1, ELK4, and GABPA binding sites can impact expression of downstream genes in F1 somatic tissue.
source: DNA methylation reduces the affinity of all three of these factors for their binding sites (Yin et al., 2017), implying that persistent hypermethylation at these sites can impact expression of downstream genes in F1 somatic tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of enriched TF binding sites in persistent DMRs and the known effect of DNA methylation on TF binding.

claim: Four of ten differentially expressed genes in healthy Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were targets of RUNX2.
source: In keeping with our prediction, four of ten differentially expressed genes in healthy Kdm6a F1 bone marrow and 134 of 1404 differentially expressed genes in diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were targets of the hematopoiesis-associated transcription factor RUNX2, a direct target of ELK1 (p=0.00492 and p=0.00102 for healthy and diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, respectively, Fisher's exact test) (Matys et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and citations.

claim: One hundred and thirty-four of 1404 differentially expressed genes in diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were targets of RUNX2.
source: In keeping with our prediction, four of ten differentially expressed genes in healthy Kdm6a F1 bone marrow and 134 of 1404 differentially expressed genes in diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were targets of the hematopoiesis-associated transcription factor RUNX2, a direct target of ELK1 (p=0.00492 and p=0.00102 for healthy and diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, respectively, Fisher's exact test) (Matys et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and citations.

claim: RUNX2 is a direct target of ELK1.
source: In keeping with our prediction, four of ten differentially expressed genes in healthy Kdm6a F1 bone marrow and 134 of 1404 differentially expressed genes in diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow were targets of the hematopoiesis-associated transcription factor RUNX2, a direct target of ELK1 (p=0.00492 and p=0.00102 for healthy and diseased Kdm6a F1 bone marrow, respectively, Fisher's exact test) (Matys et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Matys et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: An ELK1 binding site in the first intron of Runx2 falls within a persistent hypermethylated DMR.
source: An ELK1 binding site in the first intron of Runx2 falls within a persistent hypermethylated DMR and exhibits increased DNA methylation in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The ELK1 binding site in the first intron of Runx2 exhibits increased DNA methylation in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow.
source: An ELK1 binding site in the first intron of Runx2 falls within a persistent hypermethylated DMR and exhibits increased DNA methylation in both Kdm6a cKO sperm and Kdm6a F1 bone marrow (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of Runx2 was decreased in diseased Kdm6a F1 compared to control F1 bone marrow.
source: Expression of Runx2 itself was decreased in diseased Kdm6a F1 compared to control F1 bone marrow (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by expression data in Figure 5D.

claim: Principal component analysis of expression data for 134 differentially expressed RUNX2 target genes placed healthy Kdm6a F1 between diseased Kdm6a F1 and control F1 bone marrow.
source: Principal component analysis of expression data for the 134 differentially expressed RUNX2 target genes placed healthy Kdm6a F1 between diseased Kdm6a F1 and control F1 bone marrow, revealing potential underlying similarities in regulation of the Runx2 transcriptional network among Kdm6a F1 samples (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PCA data in Figure 5E.

claim: Altered regulation of transcriptional networks downstream of DNA methylation-sensitive transcription factors could result from persistent DNA hypermethylation transmitted from the Kdm6a cKO germ line to F1 somatic tissue.
source: Although the observed effect was small and should be confirmed in additional tissues, this result implies that altered regulation of transcriptional networks downstream of DNA methylation-sensitive transcription factors could result from persistent DNA hypermethylation transmitted from the Kdm6a cKO germ line to F1 somatic tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of altered RUNX2 target gene expression in Kdm6a F1 bone marrow.

claim: Loss of Kdm6a results in extensive redistribution of the H3K27me3 mark during male germ cell development.
source: We propose a model (Figure 6) wherein loss of Kdm6a results in extensive redistribution of the H3K27me3 mark during male germ cell development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Retention of H3K27me3 at regions where it would ordinarily be turned over leaves some loci vulnerable to DNA methylation.
source: Retention of H3K27me3 at regions where it would ordinarily be turned over leaves some of these loci vulnerable to DNA methylation, leading to hypermethylation in sperm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of a proposed model.

claim: Some hypermethylated regions may resist reprogramming during early embryogenesis, such that methylation persists in somatic tissue during development.
source: Early in embryogenesis, when most DNA methylation is removed from the paternal genome, some of these hypermethylated regions may resist reprogramming, such that methylation persists in somatic tissue during development; alternatively, hypermethylation may be lost at these loci during reprogramming and reestablished later in development following transmission through an epigenetic intermediate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative explanation for the persistence of DNA methylation changes.

claim: Hypermethylation may be lost during reprogramming and reestablished later in development following transmission through an epigenetic intermediate.
source: Early in embryogenesis, when most DNA methylation is removed from the paternal genome, some of these hypermethylated regions may resist reprogramming, such that methylation persists in somatic tissue during development; alternatively, hypermethylation may be lost at these loci during reprogramming and reestablished later in development following transmission through an epigenetic intermediate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an alternative speculative explanation for the persistence of DNA methylation changes.

claim: When hypermethylated regions coincide with functional enhancers, the altered epigenetic state inherited from the paternal gamete can have transcriptional consequences.
source: When these regions coincide with functional enhancers, the altered epigenetic state inherited from the paternal gamete can have transcriptional consequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: The relatively modest shift in DNA methylation levels reflects variability among individual sperm.
source: Importantly, because each sperm carries only one copy of a given locus, the relatively modest shift we observe in DNA methylation levels must reflect variability among individual sperm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of modest changes in DNA methylation at the population level.

claim: Variability in DNA methylation among individual sperm is consistent with the heterogeneous tumor profiles and other pathological phenotypes seen in the F1 population.
source: Such variability is consistent with the heterogeneous tumor profiles and other pathological phenotypes seen in our F1 population.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed variability in DNA methylation to the phenotypic variability in F1 mice.

claim: The effects of DNA methylation on downstream gene regulation manifest as a shift in the probability of transcription factor binding.
source: Similarly, in F1 somatic tissues, we propose that the effects of DNA methylation on downstream gene regulation manifest as a shift in the probability of transcription factor binding, resulting in subtle changes to transcriptional networks that impact tissue function only in the context of stressors, or cumulatively over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: Subtle changes to transcriptional networks impact tissue function only in the context of stressors, or cumulatively over time.
source: Similarly, in F1 somatic tissues, we propose that the effects of DNA methylation on downstream gene regulation manifest as a shift in the probability of transcription factor binding, resulting in subtle changes to transcriptional networks that impact tissue function only in the context of stressors, or cumulatively over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: It will be important to define the role of Uty, the Y-linked homolog of Kdm6a that lacks histone demethylase activity, in this phenomenon.
source: First, it will be important to define the role of Uty, the Y-linked homolog of Kdm6a that lacks histone demethylase activity, in this phenomenon (Hong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key question for future research.

claim: Additional developmental phenotypes may be affected in Kdm6a progeny beyond adult cancer phenotypes.
source: Second, while we have focused on adult cancer phenotypes, it is possible that additional developmental phenotypes are also affected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possibility for future investigation.

claim: Some developmental anomalies were observed in adult Kdm6a progeny, including ectopic tissue rests, tail kinks, scoliosis, and a thyroglossal duct cyst.
source: We did observe some developmental anomalies in adult Kdm6a progeny, including ectopic tissue rests, tail kinks, scoliosis, and a thyroglossal duct cyst.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on observations during the study.

claim: The extent to which premature appearance of age-associated tumors might reflect a more generalized premature aging phenotype should be examined in more depth.
source: Third, the extent to which premature appearance of age-associated tumors might reflect a more generalized premature aging phenotype should be examined in more depth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a question for future research.

claim: It will be critical to dissect the underlying molecular mechanism in more detail.
source: It will be critical to dissect the underlying molecular mechanism in more detail.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a priority for future research.

claim: DNA methylation changes induced during spermatogenesis may persist during reprogramming in the early embryo.
source: While we suggest that DNA methylation changes induced during spermatogenesis persist during reprogramming in the early embryo, we have not yet directly demonstrated that this is the case.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis that has not yet been directly tested.

claim: Epigenetic information may be transmitted through an alternative chromatin mark or RNA intermediate to reestablish DNA hypermethylation later in development.
source: It is also possible that DNA hypermethylation is lost during reprogramming, but that epigenetic information is transmitted through an alternative chromatin mark or RNA intermediate to reestablish DNA hypermethylation later in development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Assessment of DNA methylation in early Kdm6a F1 embryos will help to resolve the question of whether DNA methylation persists through reprogramming.
source: Assessment of DNA methylation in early Kdm6a F1 embryos will help to resolve this question.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed experiment to test the hypothesis.

claim: The relationship between Kdm6a loss, redistribution of H3K27me3, and gain of DNA methylation remains to be defined.
source: The relationship between Kdm6a loss, redistribution of H3K27me3, and gain of DNA methylation also remains to be defined.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an open question.

claim: The simplest explanation for the data is that dysregulation of H3K27me3 leads to DNA hypermethylation at vulnerable loci.
source: The simplest explanation for our data is that dysregulation of H3K27me3 leads to DNA hypermethylation at vulnerable loci, but it is also possible that KDM6A acts through an independent mechanism to regulate DNA methylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the simplest interpretation of the data.

claim: KDM6A may act through an independent mechanism to regulate DNA methylation.
source: The simplest explanation for our data is that dysregulation of H3K27me3 leads to DNA hypermethylation at vulnerable loci, but it is also possible that KDM6A acts through an independent mechanism to regulate DNA methylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an alternative possibility.

claim: Determination of the stage of spermatogenesis at which the observed changes in H3K27me3 and DNA methylation first appear will help to delineate the relationship between the different epigenetic consequences of Kdm6a loss.
source: Determination of the stage of spermatogenesis (proliferating spermatogonia, meiotic spermatocytes, or haploid spermatids) at which the observed changes in H3K27me3 and DNA methylation first appear will help to delineate the relationship between the different epigenetic consequences of Kdm6a loss.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed experiment to understand the mechanism.

claim: A recent study of H3K27me3 in mouse embryonic stem cells grown in 2i compared to serum-containing media described flattening of H3K27me3 signal very similar to the effect observed in Kdm6a cKO sperm.
source: Intriguingly, a recent study of H3K27me3 in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) grown in 2i compared to serum-containing media described flattening of H3K27me3 signal very similar to the effect we observed in Kdm6a cKO sperm (van Mierlo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to van Mierlo et al., 2019.

claim: In 2i mESCs, H3K27me3 flattening was associated with altered DNA methylation.
source: In 2i mESCs, H3K27me3 flattening was also associated with altered DNA methylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the cited study.

claim: A critical experiment will be to examine the sperm of Kdm6a F1s to test the prediction that changes in DNA methylation at persistent DMRs are amplified in the second generation of gametes.
source: Finally, a critical experiment will be to examine the sperm of Kdm6a F1s to test the prediction that changes in DNA methylation at persistent DMRs are amplified in the second generation of gametes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed experiment to test a key prediction of the model.

claim: At least two persistent DMRs are located in or near genes encoding components of the DNA methylation machinery (Dnmt3a and Tdg).
source: At least two persistent DMRs are located in or near genes encoding components of the DNA methylation machinery (Dnmt3a and Tdg), raising the possibility that DNA hypermethylation at these sites in sperm amplifies the changes in DNA methylation in offspring.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on analysis of persistent DMR locations.

claim: DNA hypermethylation at persistent DMRs in or near Dnmt3a and Tdg may amplify the changes in DNA methylation in offspring.
source: At least two persistent DMRs are located in or near genes encoding components of the DNA methylation machinery (Dnmt3a and Tdg), raising the possibility that DNA hypermethylation at these sites in sperm amplifies the changes in DNA methylation in offspring.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility.

claim: Dnmt3a is frequently mutated in hematological tumors and has been defined as an important tumor suppressor.
source: Dnmt3a is frequently mutated in hematological tumors and has been defined as an important tumor suppressor (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: The study was restricted to progeny of a single male founder to limit genetic variation and reduce the potential contribution of genetic heterogeneity.
source: We restricted our study to progeny of a single male founder in order to limit the amount of genetic variation in the experiment and thereby reduce the potential contribution of genetic heterogeneity, given a moderate number of experimental animals (~100 F1s and F2s total).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a justification for the experimental design.

claim: The findings should be tested in a larger study including several founder males.
source: However, our findings should be tested in a larger study including several founder males.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a recommendation for future research.

claim: A larger study would allow recovery of more diseased samples for transcriptional analysis.
source: Likewise, a larger study would allow recovery of more diseased samples for transcriptional analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a benefit of a larger study.

claim: It will be critical to exclude the possibility that loss of KDM6A in the male germ line leads to increased DNA damage and accumulation of genomic mutations that could contribute to a tumor phenotype in the next generation.
source: It will also be critical to exclude the possibility that loss of KDM6A in the male germ line leads to increased DNA damage and accumulation of genomic mutations that could contribute to a tumor phenotype in the next generation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an important control experiment.

claim: The normal spermatogenesis and fertility of Kdm6a cKO mice argue against a strong mutator phenotype.
source: Since increased DNA damage during spermatogenesis frequently leads to meiotic arrest and impaired fertility, the normal spermatogenesis and fertility of Kdm6a cKO mice argue against a strong mutator phenotype (Hunt and Hassold, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as evidence against a mutator phenotype, with a citation to Hunt and Hassold, 2002.

claim: A more subtle mutator effect should be ruled out by sequencing of genomic DNA in multiple F1 progeny and careful assessment of mutation rates.
source: However, a more subtle effect should be ruled out by sequencing of genomic DNA in multiple F1 progeny and careful assessment of mutation rates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed experiment to rule out a subtle mutator effect.

claim: Virtually nothing is known about the contribution of epigenetic perturbations in the male germ line to human disease susceptibility.
source: Virtually nothing is known about the contribution of epigenetic perturbations in the male germ line to human disease susceptibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The role of mutations that arise in the male germ line but are not transmitted to the next generation is entirely unknown and unexplored.
source: Specifically, while increased attention is being paid to the possible impacts of diet and environmental exposure on male fertility and epigenetic inheritance (Anway et al., 2005; Carone et al., 2010; Kaati et al., 2002; Ly et al., 2017), the role of mutations that arise in the male germ line but are not transmitted to the next generation is entirely unknown and unexplored.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Spermatogenic stem cells continue to divide and to accumulate de novo mutations throughout a man's lifetime.
source: Spermatogenic stem cells continue to divide and to accumulate de novo mutations throughout a man's lifetime.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as established knowledge.

claim: De novo germline mutations linked to advanced paternal age have been implicated in the pathogenesis of autism and schizophrenia.
source: De novo germline mutations linked to advanced paternal age have been implicated in the pathogenesis of autism and schizophrenia; in these cases, the causative mutations arise in the germ line and are inherited by the affected progeny (Awadalla et al., 2010; de Kluiver et al., 2017; Girard et al., 2011; Iossifov et al., 2014; Nybo Andersen and Urhoj, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: De novo mutations in the male germ line in genes such as Kdm6a may have phenotypic consequences for progeny, even when they are not inherited.
source: Our results imply that de novo mutations in the male germ line in genes such as Kdm6a may have phenotypic consequences for progeny, even when they are not inherited.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an implication of the study's findings.

claim: Intergenerational paternal effects on development have been reported for heterozygous autosomal mutations in genes encoding chromatin regulators in the mouse.
source: Intergenerational paternal effects on development have also been reported for heterozygous autosomal mutations in genes encoding chromatin regulators in the mouse (Chong et al., 2007), suggesting that the effects of non-inherited paternal germline mutations do not depend on complete loss of gene function in the germ cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chong et al., 2007.

claim: The effects of non-inherited paternal germline mutations do not depend on complete loss of gene function in the germ cells.
source: Intergenerational paternal effects on development have also been reported for heterozygous autosomal mutations in genes encoding chromatin regulators in the mouse (Chong et al., 2007), suggesting that the effects of non-inherited paternal germline mutations do not depend on complete loss of gene function in the germ cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study.

claim: A paternal age effect has been reported for ALL.
